summary: A developer can start building the Python LangChain + DocumentDB sample now: the local runtime (python, pip), cluster access mechanism (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and database name (sample_banking_11) are specified and available; vector-capable cluster features (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) are stated in the run environment. However the environment lacks the documented agent skills and MCP/tooling accelerators that speed development and provide canonical examples, and many service-level facts in the cold answers could not be verified because no documentation or MCP skills are installed. The build is feasible with workarounds but the agent will need to make several explicit choices (embedding model & dims, LLM provider, exact create_index parameters, driver/version) and test those against the live cluster.
summary_points: Build can begin: python/pip, node/npx, docker and an Azure sign-in are present and the run environment states DOCUMENTDB_URI and database name sample_banking_11.

Run environment (skill.md) confirms the cluster is vector-capable (M30, MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol, DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) and instructs reading the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI — these are the only strongly grounded facts.

No DocumentDB-specific MCP skills or documentation servers are installed (installed_skills and mcp_servers are empty), so most cold answers could not be independently verified by tools on this machine.

Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit, DocumentDB MCP Toolkit, Azure/learn MCP servers) would speed indexing, query and schema work; their absence is not blocking but slows development and increases risk of subtle mistakes.

Several implementation choices are unspecified (embedding model & dimension, LLM model/provider, exact pymongo driver/version and exact vector-createIndex parameters) and must be decided and tested against the live cluster.

Recommended immediate actions: add the DocumentDB Agent Kit skill and an official documentation MCP server, choose and pin embedding/LLM providers, and create an idempotent seed script to validate index creation against the live cluster.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the sample code, LangChain agent, seed scripts and tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or test the sample; core language runtime missing.
tools.workaround: None practical; install a supported Python runtime.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install Python dependencies (pymongo, langchain, embeddings/LLM client libraries).
tools.detail: pip available through Python virtual environment (inventory states python/pip resolve to a venv).
tools.workaround: Use system package manager to install pip or use poetry/venv tools if available.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Install MCP skills, run Node-based MCP servers, install DocumentDB Agent Kit skill if used.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot easily add or run MCP-based accelerators or Node-based tools.

tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1; extension cosmosdb-preview present (partial 'documentd' extension name in inventory).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to inspect or verify Azure-side metadata and resource configuration from the machine.
tools.workaround: Use Azure Portal or another machine with az installed. For this sample the cluster is provided and azure writes are disallowed by run policy.

tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run local MongoDB containers for local-only tests and development.

tools.name: mongosh

tools.name: DocumentDB Agent Kit (accelerator)
tools.needed_for: Provides agent skills and canonical examples for data modeling, indexing and vector search; speeds correct index creation and query examples.
tools.impact_if_missing: No authoritative, pre-built code examples or sample index creation scripts from the agent kit; higher risk of using non-recommended index parameters or API variants.
tools.workaround: Follow the run environment guidance and author index creation and queries by hand, then test against the cluster. Install the kit via npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit to get canonical examples.

tools.name: Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit (accelerator)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane tools: query, aggregate, index management, schema inspection tailored to DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: No ready-made data-plane tooling on the MCP to query or inspect the live cluster; more manual verification required.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI and hand-written Python scripts (pymongo) to inspect indexes and data. Add the MCP entry 'documentdb' in mcp.json to enable the toolkit.

tools.name: Microsoft Learn MCP Server (documentation search)
tools.needed_for: Quick, canonical access to Learn docs for accurate, versioned guidance.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent cannot query official Learn docs via the MCP; documentation lookups must be done manually in a browser.
tools.workaround: Open official Learn docs in a browser; add the MCP entry learn in mcp.json to enable programmatic lookups.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: No installed documentation or MCP skill to confirm whether the managed DocumentDB product uses the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider name or a different resource type; the cold answer matches historical Cosmos DB names but we could not verify current canonical resource-provider naming.
confusions.build_risk: If the resource provider or type is assumed incorrectly, any automation that tried to look up or document the managed cluster via ARM/Bicep/Terraform could fail or target the wrong resource type when the builder attempts to inspect Azure-side metadata.
improvements: Add a canonical statement in the public docs and the agent kit that lists the resource provider and exact resource type for the managed DocumentDB cluster (e.g. on a Learn quickstart page).
Ensure the DocumentDB Agent Kit includes an example az CLI command that shows the exact resource type returned by 'az resource show' for the cluster.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: az cosmosdb (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer appears to describe the Cosmos DB 'az cosmosdb' CLI group which historically managed Cosmos DB accounts (including Mongo API). Without the docs/MCP server we cannot verify whether the managed DocumentDB product uses the exact same CLI group or requires a new/preview extension command.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong az command or assuming the operation is in core CLI when it requires a preview extension could break automated setup or developer workflows that inspect the account.
improvements: Document the exact preferred az CLI command group for this managed DocumentDB product in the agent kit and in Learn quickstarts, and indicate if it is in core az or requires an extension (and the extension name).
Put a short example 'az cosmosdb show' call in the sample README that the builder can run to confirm the account.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (and child types Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongodbCollections). Terraform (azurerm): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account, plus azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for MongoDB DBs/collections.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer uses the historical Cosmos resource names and azurerm provider types; without authoritative docs or the MCP infra skill we cannot confirm that the new managed 'Azure DocumentDB' service maps to the exact same ARM resource names or Terraform resources.
confusions.build_risk: If an IaC template targets the wrong resource types, it will fail or provision the wrong service; however provisioning is not required for this sample under the run policy.
improvements: Add an explicit 'deploy with Bicep/Terraform' section in Learn and the agent kit showing the exact resource provider/resource type and a minimal example template for the DocumentDB cluster.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Standard MongoDB connection string. Example (direct): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000. SRV form also works for supported accounts: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The example matches known Cosmos DB Mongo API connection strings (host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255), but we have no installed documentation or tooling to confirm whether the managed DocumentDB cluster uses identical hostnames/ports or a different host suffix/port scheme.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the wrong host suffix, port or required connection options they may not be able to connect to the cluster. Because the run environment guarantees DOCUMENTDB_URI is present, the practical impact is low if the builder reads that env var, but any documentation or templates that recompose the connection string may be wrong.
improvements: In the run environment docs and agent kit, include the canonical example of the expected connection string format and a note to always read DOCUMENTDB_URI rather than constructing the connection string from parts.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is Azure Cosmos DB Request Units (RU/s) with provisioned throughput or serverless (pay-per-RU) where available. There is also a newer dedicated/vCore-style offering for some MongoDB-compatible SKUs (M-series) in some regions, but the common model is RU-based or serverless for Cosmos Mongo API.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: This answer mixes historical Cosmos DB RU-based billing and references to vCore-style offerings; without docs the exact billing model for the managed DocumentDB offering (which the run environment labels as compute tier M30) cannot be confirmed.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample makes assumptions about RU quotas or indexes that are expensive, the developer might mischaracterize costs in the README, but the sample is being run against an existing cluster so billing changes do not block the build.
improvements: Add a concise pricing/capacity paragraph in Learn and the agent kit that states whether the managed DocumentDB SKU is billed by RUs, vCores, or both for the offered tiers, and call out which tiers support vector indexes.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane access for the MongoDB API is typically done with MongoDB credentials (username/password) derived from the account keys and provided in the MongoDB connection string (SCRAM-based auth). Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB API data plane; drivers should use the connection string credentials and TLS.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: This reflects the common situation for Cosmos Mongo API accounts historically, but we could not confirm whether the managed DocumentDB data plane adds Entra ID auth or other auth modes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to use Entra ID auth when it is not supported the connection will fail; conversely, if Entra ID is supported but the sample uses account keys the setup may be non-idiomatic for some customers.
improvements: Add a clear statement in the agent kit and the run environment docs enumerating supported authentication methods for the MongoDB-compatible data plane and an example of how to use Entra ID if it is supported.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo). Do not use the Cosmos DB SQL/core SDK for MongoDB API workloads; the MongoDB wire protocol compatible drivers are the correct clients.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer follows the conventional guidance for MongoDB-compatible endpoints; without agent-kit docs we could not verify whether the product team intends a dedicated service-specific SDK or to continue recommending standard MongoDB drivers.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses the wrong client library it may miss product-specific features or produce suboptimal behavior; however using pymongo is the typical choice and likely to work with the MongoDB wire protocol specified in the run environment.
improvements: Add a short sentence in the agent kit README confirming the recommended client library (pymongo for Python) and a pinned example dependency line.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Index types include typical vector index families (example: hnsw, ivf, diskann) on vector-capable clusters. The MongoDB 7-style createIndex syntax is used. Example command: db.getCollection('profiles').createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', dimensions: 1536, 'similarity': 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: The run environment (skill.md) states the reachable cluster is vector-capable and supports DiskANN, HNSW and IVF index types on MongoDB 7.0 wire-protocol clusters; exact createIndex parameters are not provided in the run environment and must be tested against the cluster driver. (Grounding from run environment text.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer provides an example that matches MongoDB 7's knnVector index syntax and parameters, but the run environment only confirmed which index families are supported (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) and did not supply the precise createIndex options (names of options, exact parameter names or which 'similarity' options are accepted). The example may be syntactically correct for upstream MongoDB 7 but needs verification against the managed cluster.
confusions.build_risk: Using untested index-creation parameters may cause index creation to fail, produce suboptimal indexing behaviour, or mismatch the embedding dimension expected by the index and the embeddings produced by the model.
improvements: Include a concrete, copy-paste createIndex example in the DocumentDB Agent Kit showing the exact syntax and options to create an HNSW (or other) vector index against the managed cluster.
Add a short test script in the agent kit that creates the index against the provided cluster and verifies the index exists, so sample builders can run it deterministically.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Basic full‑text search can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field:'text'})). For richer/full-featured hybrid/vector+text search you typically combine vector queries with text filtering on the DB side or integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for advanced hybrid ranking; there is no separate built-in Cosmos 'hybrid search' engine for MongoDB API beyond text indexes and vector operators.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes MongoDB text index behavior with hybrid search approaches (including Azure Cognitive Search, which is a separate product). We could not verify whether the managed DocumentDB product offers an integrated hybrid ranking engine or whether hybrid searches should be implemented by combining vector queries + text filters in the DB.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a specific hybrid search capability that is not present, the sample's search quality or the query method will be incorrect; however the sample can implement vector search + text filtering client-side as a safe default.
improvements: Document the recommended approach for hybrid search in the agent kit: either using DB-native vector + text filters or integrating with Azure Cognitive Search, with an example for the sample.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Clusters advertise a MongoDB wire protocol version mapped to a server version (recent Cosmos Mongo API deployments support MongoDB 6.0 and 7.0 feature levels on newer clusters). However, not all MongoDB features are implemented identically; historically there have been gaps (some aggregation stages, server-side JS/eval, certain transaction semantics and advanced replication features). Expect to use standard drivers but validate advanced features (multi-shard transactions, some change-stream/aggregation behaviors) against the target cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: The run environment explicitly states the provided cluster uses MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (grounding: run environment text). Specific unsupported features are not enumerated in the run environment, so feature gaps could not be verified.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The answer mixes general remarks about differences between Cosmos DB's Mongo API and upstream MongoDB; the run environment confirms the MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol but does not list feature omissions. Thus parts of the cold answer are likely but not verifiable from the materials.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses advanced features that the managed cluster does not implement, runtime errors will occur. The safe approach is to test the exact operations against the live cluster.
improvements: Add a concise compatibility matrix in the agent kit listing supported MongoDB server features and any known limitations for the advertised MongoDB 7.0 compatibility on the managed cluster.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full emulator that perfectly reproduces the MongoDB API on Cosmos. For local development use the official MongoDB server Docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) and expose port 27017: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:7.0. For Cosmos-specific features test against a real Cosmos DB account since the emulator targets the SQL/core API only.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is a reasonable general recommendation but we could not verify whether the agent kit or docs recommend a specific image or provide a managed DocumentDB-local compatibility image; the run environment explicitly said 'no local DocumentDB gateway is running' and to verify against the live cluster.
confusions.build_risk: Relying solely on a local mongo:7.0 image may not reproduce managed-cluster-specific behavior; the run environment explicitly requires verification against the live cluster, so the sample must include integration or system tests that target the provided account.
improvements: Explicitly state in the agent kit that local mongo:7.0 is only an approximation and provide guidance on which behaviors must be validated against the live cluster.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported when the cluster exposes a MongoDB wire protocol version that includes them; no special tenant toggle is normally required, but support has depended on the API/version of the account. In practice, use the driver's watch() API against the collection; if the account/version doesn't support change streams the driver will error.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer tracks upstream MongoDB behavior and historical variations in managed APIs, but we have no authoritative documentation here to confirm whether change streams are enabled on this managed DocumentDB product by default.
confusions.build_risk: If change streams are assumed available and they are not, runtime errors will occur. The safe approach is to test watch() against the live cluster.
improvements: Document change-stream support and any required account flags in the agent kit, with a short test snippet that calls watch() and explains expected errors if unsupported.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: My expectation: the general Azure MCP/agents that manage Cosmos DB data-plane tasks are covered by the standard Azure management/control plane; there is not a separate special-purpose MCP server special-case for DocumentDB beyond the normal Azure management stack. (Low confidence — details vary by internal Microsoft infra.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: No MCP servers or documentation servers are installed to confirm which MCP server covers data-plane tools for this managed DocumentDB offering. The known_accelerators mention an Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit and an Azure MCP server entry but neither is installed.
confusions.build_risk: Without the MCP toolkit the agent has to hand-roll index, query and schema inspection routines; the build is slowed and there's higher chance of using non-recommended commands.
improvements: Add the DocumentDB MCP Toolkit and Learn MCP Server to the default agent kit configuration and document which MCP server provides which capabilities.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's JSON document database service; it was rebranded/merged into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos exposes multiple APIs, one of which is the original DocumentDB/SQL API and another is the MongoDB-compatible API. The open-source DocumentDB project is unrelated; the Azure product is not the same as any separate open-source repository named DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: The prompt review and run environment materials indicate that naming has been a source of confusion: the managed MongoDB-compatible service is being referred to as 'Azure DocumentDB' (this repo's definition). Historically 'DocumentDB' was the precursor to Cosmos DB; the relationship and naming may vary in older docs. (Grounding: prompt_review and run environment text.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is aligned with the prompt and prompt_review which explicitly discuss naming and neighbouring products; the run materials highlighted these common confusions.
confusions.build_risk: Low for the sample itself, but inconsistent naming in docs could confuse readers and cause them to use wrong driver docs or other products' documentation.
improvements: Enforce the name 'Azure DocumentDB' across the sample README and include a short note in the top-level README clarifying the relationship to Cosmos DB (former name) and the open-source DocumentDB project.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Microsoft/Azure's proprietary Cosmos DB engine implementing the MongoDB wire protocol for the MongoDB API. In most cases application code using standard MongoDB drivers will work, but expect behavioral and feature differences (throughput billed as RUs, some unsupported operators/stages, differences in transactions/consistency and certain admin commands).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects historical Cosmos DB architecture and its MongoDB-compat layer; without installed docs or agent kit we cannot confirm whether the new managed DocumentDB product uses the exact same engine or has a different underlying implementation.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes exact parity with upstream MongoDB behavior it may exercise features that behave differently on the managed cluster; the recommended mitigation is to validate operations against the live cluster.
improvements: Provide a short 'compatibility notes' section in the agent kit and README describing engine differences and listing commonly mismatched commands or behaviors to watch for.

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_banking_11 for all created collections and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use database name sample_banking_11 — this is stated in the run environment (skill.md).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the run environment explicitly provides this name.
confusions.build_risk: Low — following this avoids accidental reads/writes to other DBs.

confusions.question: Which environment variable contains the cluster connection string for this sample?
confusions.cold_answer: DOCUMENTDB_URI — read this at runtime (do not hard-code). Use it directly with MongoClient in the app.
confusions.grounded_answer: DOCUMENTDB_URI is the designated environment variable per the run environment (skill.md). The run environment also instructs never to write its value to files or logs. (Grounding: run environment text.)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — explicitly stated in the run environment.
confusions.build_risk: Low provided the builder reads DOCUMENTDB_URI and never commits secrets.

confusions.question: Which client library and commands will the sample use to create a vector index and run vector queries?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo (official MongoDB Python driver). Create a vector index with collection.create_index({ 'embedding': 'knnVector' }, { 'dimensions': 1536, 'similarity': 'cosine', 'method': { 'name': 'hnsw', 'm': 16, 'efConstruction': 200 } }). Use find with $vectorSearch or the MongoDB 7 vector query operator to retrieve nearest neighbors.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer provides a plausible MongoDB 7-style approach and pymongo is a natural library, but the run environment did not specify the Python driver or exact index creation syntax. Without agent-kit examples or docs we cannot confirm exact driver usage or the operator name for vector queries on this managed cluster.
confusions.build_risk: If the driver or operator names differ from the example, index creation or vector queries will fail at runtime. The safe approach is to test index creation and queries with small test scripts against the provided cluster.
improvements: Add a concrete code snippet in the agent kit that shows how to create the vector index using the recommended Python driver and how to run the vector query syntax against the managed cluster.

confusions.question: What collection schema and indexes will the sample create?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a collection 'profiles' in sample_banking_11. Documents include _id, name, metadata, embedding (array of floats, length 1536). Indexes: vector knnVector index on embedding (dimensions=1536, similarity=cosine, method=hnsw) and a text index on 'metadata' or 'adverse_media' fields for hybrid searches.
confusions.grounded_answer: partly_wrong — the run environment prescribes the DB name and that vector indexes (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) are supported, but it does not specify collection names, embedding dimension or exact schema. The collection name 'profiles' and a 1536-dim embedding are reasonable defaults but are not grounded in the provided materials.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer fills gaps (collection name and embedding dims) that the run environment intentionally left unspecified; those choices are implementation decisions rather than canonical facts.
confusions.build_risk: If the embedding dimension does not match the chosen embedding model the index will fail or be invalid. Using an untested schema may cause integration mismatches with downstream code.
improvements: Specify the collection names and example document schema in the agent kit and include a .env.example entry that lists the chosen embedding model and its dimension so index creation scripts use the correct dimensions.

confusions.question: How will the Python agent authenticate to the cluster in code?
confusions.cold_answer: Pass the DOCUMENTDB_URI connection string into pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True). The connection string must include username/password and options like ssl=true and replicaSet=globaldb where required.
confusions.grounded_answer: partly_wrong — the run environment instructs reading DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and not writing it to files (grounding: run environment). It does not mandate pymongo or list exact connection options; the example approach is plausible but not verified against the managed cluster's required options.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumes pymongo and the typical MongoDB URI options used by Cosmos DB's Mongo API, but the run environment didn't specify the driver or explicit connection string options.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the wrong driver options the client may fail to connect. The safe approach is to use the provided DOCUMENTDB_URI verbatim with the chosen MongoDB driver and test a connection before creating indexes or loading data.
improvements: Add a minimal code snippet to the agent kit that demonstrates creating a pymongo.MongoClient from DOCUMENTDB_URI and verifying connectivity; include recommended driver versions.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & output dimension
information_gaps.description: The prompt and run environment do not name which embedding model and provider to use (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, etc.) nor the embedding vector dimension (e.g., 1536). I looked at the prompt_review and run environment but found no model or dimension specified. The builder must choose and document this; index dimensions must match the model output.

information_gaps.title: LLM model/provider for narratives
information_gaps.description: No provider or model is specified for generating the plain-language risk narrative (e.g., OpenAI/gpt-4o-mini or Azure OpenAI). The prompt_review suggested choices but no authoritative selection is present in the materials searched (prompt_review and run environment).

information_gaps.title: Exact Python MongoDB driver & pinned version
information_gaps.description: The run environment does not specify which MongoDB driver/package or version to use (pymongo or other). I checked the run environment and inventory; no pinned driver version or dependency list was provided.

information_gaps.title: Concrete createIndex syntax for managed cluster
information_gaps.description: The run environment states vector index families (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) are supported but does not provide exact createIndex parameter names and example code for the managed service. Without the agent kit or docs the exact parameter names and permitted options are unknown.

information_gaps.title: Seed/sample data files
information_gaps.description: No sample sanctions/adverse media or correspondent profiles are included in the provided materials. The builder will need to create synthetic sample JSON/CSV files and an idempotent seed script; the run environment asked to load sample data but did not supply it.

information_gaps.title: Risk score calculation method
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires returning a risk score but gives no formula or guidance for deriving scores from similarity results (e.g., scaling of similarity to risk, aggregation of multiple matches). The materials searched (prompt_review and run environment) do not supply a scoring heuristic.

information_gaps.title: Unit test mocking strategy
information_gaps.description: No guidance is present about how to design unit tests that run without a live cluster (e.g., how to mock pymongo, embedding calls). The run environment says to verify against the live cluster but does not provide testing or mocking examples.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the database name sample_banking_11 for all collections and operations (do not write to other databases).
Read the DocumentDB connection string from the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime and never write the raw secret into files, logs, or repository artifacts.

The target cluster is vector-capable and advertises DiskANN, HNSW and IVF index families on MongoDB 7.0 wire-protocol clusters; test any createIndex parameters against the live cluster before relying on them in the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH to allow interactive verification of connectivity, indexes and documents; simplest install is to use the official MongoDB download appropriate for the platform or 'npm install -g mongosh'.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because provisioning is disallowed by run policy; add azd only if you plan to add template-based deployment tests on a separate machine.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for this sample because the cluster is pre-provisioned and azure_writes_allowed is false; include Bicep examples in the repo instead of requiring the CLI locally.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for the current run policy; if the team wants IaC tests, make terraform available on a separate CI agent instead.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Python LangChain sample; not worth adding for this build.
